content.jointProblem: Can deterministic finite automaton models, inferred passively from each site's own normal Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP traffic, serve as per-site behavioural baselines that flag drift with a false-positive rate plant operators tolerate, and can the flagged message sequences be explained to a plant manager in plain language? The first experiment tests whether the automaton detector transfers from a test-environment SCADA protocol dataset with injected anomalies to ArmaturaSec's real Modbus/BACnet captures.

rationale.text: Hadžić's core method is anomaly detection from normal traffic only: an automaton inferred from normal traffic acts as the baseline and messages causing transitions absent from the model are flagged, which matches a setting with zero labelled attacks.

sources.quote: Once a finite automaton model of a protocol is inferred from normal traffic, it can serve as a baseline for anomaly detection
messages causing transitions absent from the model are flagged

rationale.text: She has already evaluated this principle on SCADA protocol sessions with injected anomalies, reporting precision 0.91 and recall 0.87 averaged across five anomaly types.

sources.quote: The inferred DFA correctly flags anomalous sessions with a precision of 0.91 and a recall of 0.87 averaged across anomaly types.

rationale.text: She brings learning-theoretic guarantees for the one-sided error case that a safety-oriented ICS detector needs, where the model may miss anomalies but must not accept out-of-language behaviour.

sources.quote: the hypothesis may reject strings in the target language but must not accept strings outside it
This one-sided error condition arises naturally in safety-critical protocol verification.

rationale.text: The inference tooling already exists as an open-source Python library implementing seven algorithms, so feasibility work can start from a working codebase rather than from scratch.

sources.quote: GInferLib, an open-source Python library providing implementations of seven grammatical inference algorithms for deterministic and nondeterministic finite automata

rationale.text: She has prior industrial experience on an anomaly detection pilot for SCADA protocol traffic with an embedded systems company, contributing inference algorithms and evaluation methodology.

sources.quote: Hadžić collaborated with BEZ Systems d.o.o., a Novi Sad-based embedded systems company, on an anomaly detection pilot for SCADA protocol traffic between 2018 and 2020

rationale.text: Her running project already lists a verified automaton-based anomaly detector for industrial control system traffic as a secondary objective, so this task aligns with an existing research direction.

sources.quote: A secondary objective is producing a verified automaton-based anomaly detector applicable to industrial control system traffic.

rationale.text: She is explicitly open to joint company projects on protocol analysis and network security.

sources.quote: joint projects with companies on protocol analysis or network security

constraints.text: The method must work with no malicious examples at all: no confirmed attack captures exist, and supervised classifiers trained on public ICS data have already failed in deployment.

sources.quote: our clients have never been breached (or don't know it), so we have zero examples of malicious traffic and supervised classifiers are useless to us
it flagged so many false positives in real deployments that clients started switching the alerts off

constraints.text: The detector has to learn a site-specific normal baseline and flag drift, not apply one global model.

sources.quote: something that learns what normal looks like on a specific site and raises a flag when behaviour drifts from that baseline

constraints.text: Training data are the multi-terabyte normal-traffic archives collected from consenting clients over three years, accessible only under NDA.

sources.quote: we have collected several terabytes of captures from consenting clients over the past three years
We can dedicate one to two engineers part-time to a collaborative project

constraints.text: Inference must run on the Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP inspection appliance, on the planned security processor, without hurting packet forwarding latency.

sources.quote: ProtoSense: passive protocol inspection module for Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP traffic
release a fifth hardware variant in late 2025 with a dedicated security processor to support on-device anomaly detection without affecting packet forwarding latency

constraints.text: Every alert must be explainable to a non-specialist plant manager in plain language.

sources.quote: we need a method that works with no attack examples and that we can explain to a plant manager in plain language

constraints.text: Company-side effort is capped: one to two engineers part-time and one engineer who has been self-studying anomaly detection for six months, with the firmware codebase available only under NDA.

sources.quote: we have one engineer who has been reading about anomaly detection for six months
with access to our traffic archives, our hardware bench, and our existing firmware codebase under NDA

risks: Transfer gap: the published detector was evaluated on 230,000 sessions of a single SCADA protocol captured in a test environment with injected anomalies, not on real Modbus TCP or BACnet/IP traffic from substations and pump stations.

Transfer gap on data regime: the evaluation used a dataset with known injected anomalies, whereas ArmaturaSec has no labelled malicious traffic, so the claimed precision and recall cannot be assumed and a defensible evaluation (testbed injection, hardware-in-the-loop bench) must be designed first.

The published method detects field mutation less reliably because such anomalies do not always alter the message-type sequence; Modbus/BACnet attacks with unchanged message sequences (e.g. register value tampering) may be missed by a pure automaton baseline.

False-positive fatigue is the historical failure mode here — a previous classifier caused clients to switch alerts off — and a drift-based flagging scheme can reproduce it on noisy twenty-year-old networks.

Passive inference is bounded by trace coverage: states and transitions absent from the training traces will be misclassified as anomalous, and the company's archives contain no deliberate exploration of protocol behaviour.
The researcher's availability and capacity are unknown, and the project plan depends on supervision time that has not been confirmed.
The company has only six months of self-study in anomaly detection and 1–2 part-time engineers, which may be thin for a research-heavy method transfer.
The one previous collaboration with a Novi Sad technical faculty produced useful code but was not continued formally, so follow-through and IP/NDA arrangements are unproven.
Explainability of automaton-based decisions to plant managers is untested; no evidence in the material shows that transition-level explanations are understandable to operations staff.
Scalability of state-merging inference to large protocol alphabets and multi-terabyte archives is an open research question even in the researcher's own project.
questions: Which Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP captures can be shared under NDA, from how many distinct sites, and do any of them contain known incidents, maintenance windows or red-team exercises that could serve as weak labels?
What false-positive rate per site per week would clients actually tolerate, and how are ProtoSense alerts triaged today?
What are the compute, memory and latency budget on the current ProtoSense hardware and on the planned security-processor variant?
Can ArmaturaSec provide the hardware-in-the-loop bench with physical PLC simulators for injecting controlled anomalies to build an evaluation set?
What is Ksenija Hadžić's availability and supervision capacity for this engagement, and over what timeframe?
Would the company also consider hosting an industrial PhD candidate under her co-supervision instead of, or alongside, a joint project?
What form of explanation does a plant manager need in practice (flagged transition, plain-language sentence, site report), and who would validate it?
How would ownership and licensing of the inference code and any resulting models be arranged, given that GInferLib is open source and the firmware is under NDA?
